demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one. Snake-related and pregnancy/birth reminders imply trauma contexts unrelated to bereavement, and there is no supporting threat or memory content linking them to this loss.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons similarly implies a trauma context involving violence, combat, or armed threat, which is unsupported by the stated trauma type and by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to justify unless the death specifically involved childbirth or infant loss; nothing else in the profile supports that context. This makes the trigger clinically implausible relative to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons implies a trauma context involving combat, assault, or armed responders. That does not fit the rest of this bereavement-focused profile and is not supported by the other trigger, threat, or strategy items, so it appears incoherent with the trauma type and overall formulation.

vignette: Ravi Patel is a 39-year-old South Asian male, an interior designer by profession, married to his high school sweetheart, Priya. Ravi’s life took a devastating turn when he lost his younger brother, Rajiv, in a sudden and unexpected car accident three years ago. The event was particularly traumatic as it occurred on their family’s annual trip to their ancestral village in India, where they would spend time with extended family and celebrate important traditions. The day of the accident was supposed to be filled with joyous reunions and shared memories, but instead, Ravi witnessed his brother being rushed away in an ambulance, never to return. Since that fateful day, Ravi has found himself haunted by vivid flashbacks of the scene—seeing Rajiv’s lifeless body lying motionless on the ground, hearing the distant wail of sirens growing closer with each passing second. These intrusive memories often leave him feeling as if he is reliving the accident in real-time. Ravi had come to believe that his body reacts to danger before he even has time to think about it. This belief was reinforced during a recent project where he had to design a funeral home’s interior, which triggered intense anxiety and panic attacks. His body would react automatically, with racing heartbeats and sweat breaking out on his forehead, as if the threat of reliving Rajiv’s accident were imminent. Since the tragedy, Ravi has been avoiding any reminders of loss and grief. He meticulously avoids anniversaries associated with the event, including the date of the accident and other significant dates related to Rajiv's life. This avoidance extends to anything that might remind him of his brother or the accident—funerals, cemeteries, even conversations about people losing loved ones. One particularly challenging moment for Ravi occurred during a family gathering on what would have been Rajiv’s birthday. He found himself unable to participate in any activities and withdrew into seclusion, struggling with the overwhelming sense of loss and grief. His irritability had increased significantly, leading to frequent outbursts at work and strained relationships with his colleagues. Ravi's attempts to mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios have left him feeling prepared but also perpetually on edge. He would spend hours imagining various catastrophic outcomes, convinced that by doing so, he could better handle any unexpected tragedies in the future. This mental rehearsal has become a coping mechanism that paradoxically increased his anxiety and sense of vulnerability. The cumulative impact of these avoidance behaviors and maladaptive strategies began to take a toll on Ravi’s work and personal life. His avoidance led him to decline several high-profile projects, fearing they might trigger memories or feelings associated with the accident. This resulted in financial strain and mounting pressure from his employer, further exacerbating his stress. What frightened Ravi most was the fear of losing control and being unable to manage the intense emotions that would inevitably surface during important family events or professional milestones. He became increasingly isolated, pushing away loved ones who tried to support him out of a misguided belief that they might trigger his grief. The final straw came when Priya expressed her concern about Ravi’s deteriorating mental health and suggested seeking help from a therapist. Realizing that he could no longer bear the burden alone, Ravi agreed to start therapy. He is most hoping for a way to regain control over his emotions and reconnect with his family without feeling overwhelmed by the memories of Rajiv's untimely death. Ravi’s current state reflects a deep-seated fear of losing control and being consumed by grief, but he remains hopeful that through therapy, he can find a healthier balance between remembering Rajiv and living his own life.
